incidents.title: Refund hit the wrong order
incidents.brief: ShopKart split orders across 4 MySQL shards, each with its own AUTO_INCREMENT. Order #88,213,007 now exists on two shards, and 1,900 refunds a day land on the wrong customer.
incidents.constraint: IDs must stay 64-bit BIGINTs, roughly time-sorted, and shards grow from 4 to 16 next quarter.
incidents.question: Refunds are safe for now. What stops new order IDs from colliding?

users: support: refund on #88213007 hit a different customer
api: order #88213007 returned by shard 1 and shard 3 lookup
refund lookup by order_id fans out, 2 rows matched
s1: no cross-shard uniqueness check on orders.id
s2: dup id 88213007 seen on shard 1 during reconciliation

choices.label: Snowflake IDs: 41-bit ms time, 10-bit worker, 12-bit sequence
choices.resultTitle: One ID space for every shard
choices.resultBody: Each of up to 1,024 workers mints 4,096 IDs per millisecond without asking anyone, so the 4 shards can never collide and IDs still sort by time. Cost: worker IDs must be assigned uniquely.

choices.label: Set auto_increment_increment=4 with a different offset per shard
choices.resultBody: Interleaving fixes today's 4 shards, but moving to 16 means changing the step on live tables; rows copied during the split collide again and refunds keep misrouting.

choices.label: Switch the order key to random UUIDv4 values on every shard
choices.resultTitle: Unique but too wide and random
choices.resultBody: UUIDv4 never collides, but it is 128 bits, breaking the 40 services that store BIGINT order IDs, and random inserts scatter across the B-tree so shard CPU climbs to 84%.

hints: Each shard's counter only knows about its own rows.
The constraint wants 64 bits, time order and more shards later.
Split the 64 bits into time, who generated it, and a per-millisecond counter.

mitigation.question: Refunds are landing on strangers right now. What stops the damage first?

choices.label: Refund only when order ID and customer ID both match
choices.resultBody: The refund API now rejects any order whose customer does not match the requester, so the 1,900 misroutes a day drop to zero and the rare mismatch goes to manual review. The IDs still collide underneath.

choices.label: Restart all four shards to resync their AUTO_INCREMENT counters
choices.resultBody: MySQL 8 persists each AUTO_INCREMENT value across restarts, so every shard resumes its own sequence; checkout was down for two minutes and refunds keep hitting the wrong customer.

choices.label: Freeze every refund until the duplicate orders are cleaned up
choices.resultBody: Misroutes stop, but about 28,000 legitimate refunds a day pile up, support tickets triple within hours, and card-network rules give you days, not weeks, to pay them.

incidents.title: UUID keys thrash the buffer pool
incidents.brief: PayLedger inserts 30,000 transactions/s with UUIDv4 primary keys. The buffer pool hit rate fell from 99% to 71% and p95 insert latency is 45 ms.
incidents.constraint: Keys must stay 128-bit UUIDs because partners already store them.
incidents.question: What restores insert locality without changing the key format?

api: sample PKs in arrival order: 9f3c..., 1b07..., e44a..., 52d1... (no ordering)
db: page splits 11k/s on ledger_tx PRIMARY, leaf pages ~55% full
rep: buffer pool hit 74%, applying scattered page writes

choices.label: Generate UUIDv7 keys, which put a millisecond timestamp first
choices.resultTitle: New rows land on the right edge
choices.resultBody: UUIDv7 keeps the 128-bit format partners expect, but its leading 48-bit timestamp makes the 30,000 inserts/s append to the newest index pages, so the hit rate returns to about 99%.

choices.label: Double the InnoDB buffer pool from 64 GB to 128 GB of RAM
choices.resultBody: More RAM holds more of the random pages for now, but the table grows by 2.6 billion rows a day and the working set outruns 128 GB again within weeks.

choices.label: Hash-partition the table into 16 partitions keyed by the UUID
choices.resultTitle: Sixteen random indexes instead of one
choices.resultBody: Each partition still receives uniformly random keys, so every insert touches a cold page somewhere; locality is unchanged and planning overhead adds CPU.

hints: Where in the index does each new random key land?
Sequential keys keep writes on a few hot pages.
Some UUID versions start with the creation time.

variants.constraint: Partner contracts pin keys to random UUIDv4 until a 2027 recertification. The ledger keeps only 30 days of rows, so its primary-key index stays flat at 90 GB.

more-ram.resultTitle: The whole index fits in memory
more-ram.resultBody: At 128 GB the pool holds the entire 90 GB primary-key index, so random inserts hit cached pages again: hit rate back to 99%, p95 near 7 ms. It costs $900 a month and holds because the 30-day window stops growth.

uuid-v7.resultBody: UUIDv7 would restore locality, but partner validators accept only version-4 UUIDs until 2027. Every transaction carrying a v7 key bounces at settlement, and the 90 GB index would have fit in RAM anyway.

hints: Is the index still growing, or has it stopped at a fixed size?
Random inserts only hurt when the pages they touch are not in memory.
Compare the index size with how much memory the database can cache.

incidents.title: Duplicate event IDs after NTP step
incidents.brief: An NTP correction stepped one Snowflake worker's clock back 800 ms. It re-minted IDs for timestamps it had already used, and 3,100 Kafka events were deduplicated away as repeats.
incidents.constraint: The worker must never emit the same ID twice, even when its clock jumps.
incidents.question: What change stops the duplicates?

choices.label: Track the last timestamp; wait or fail while the clock is behind
choices.resultBody: The worker compares each tick with the last millisecond it used and stalls or errors for up to 800 ms instead of reusing it; NTP is also set to slew, not step, so pauses stay rare.

choices.label: Widen the Snowflake sequence field from 12 bits to 16 bits
choices.resultBody: A wider sequence only raises IDs per millisecond. After the step the sequence resets to 0 for a timestamp already used, so the same 3,100 IDs are minted again.

choices.label: Catch duplicate-key errors in the DB and regenerate the event ID
choices.resultTitle: The duplicates never hit the DB
choices.resultBody: Kafka consumers, caches and logs see the ID before any unique index does, so events are still dropped as repeats; the DB retry only covers one of several sinks.

hints: Snowflake assumes time only moves forward.
Which bits repeat when the timestamp repeats?
Remember the last millisecond the worker issued.

gen: idgen: sequence reset to 0 for ts=1759023841121
dedupe: WARN drop event 1759023841121-17-0003: id already seen
WARN 3,100 duplicate ids in 5 min, all worker=17

culprit.explanation: Worker 17's log shows ntpd stepping its clock back 800 ms and the generator issuing timestamps below the last one it used, so it re-minted IDs it had already handed out. The dedupe consumer only noticed the repeats.

wrongNodeFeedback.dedupe: The consumer is doing its job: dropping IDs it has already seen. Where did the repeated IDs come from?
wrongNodeFeedback.q: Kafka is healthy with lag 0; it only carries the IDs it is given.

incidents.title: Two pods share worker ID 412
incidents.brief: RideNow autoscales to 220 ID-generator pods. Each picks its Snowflake worker ID as hash(pod name) mod 1024, and 0.3% of trip IDs are now duplicates.
incidents.constraint: Pods come and go every few minutes; a worker ID must never be live twice.
incidents.question: How should pods get their worker IDs?

choices.label: Lease worker IDs from etcd with a TTL renewed by heartbeat
choices.resultTitle: Each ID has exactly one owner
choices.resultBody: A pod claims a free ID with a compare-and-set lease and renews it every few seconds; if it dies the lease expires before the ID is reused. Cost: startup now depends on etcd.

choices.label: Pick a random worker ID between 0 and 1023 at pod startup
choices.resultBody: With 220 pods drawing from 1,024 slots, the chance that at least two share an ID is above 99.99%, so duplicates keep appearing on every scale-up.

choices.label: Use the last octet of the pod's IP as its worker ID
choices.resultBody: The cluster spans four /24 subnets, so 10.0.1.23 and 10.0.3.23 both become worker 23, and recycled IPs can revive an ID still in use elsewhere.

hints: Hashing 220 names into 1,024 slots is a birthday problem.
Uniqueness needs one authority, not a local guess.
Think of a claim that expires if its owner dies.

variants.constraint: All 220 pods share one /24 subnet, so the network plugin never gives two live pods the same address. The cluster has no etcd, and a new quorum means another system to run.

ip-octet.resultBody: In a single /24, IPAM hands each live pod a distinct address, so the last octet is a unique worker ID with no extra system. The cost: the group is capped at 254 pods, and a second subnet would break it.

lease-ids.resultTitle: Correct, but a new quorum to babysit
lease-ids.resultBody: Leases end the duplicates, but this cluster has no etcd, so the team now runs a 3-node quorum for $120 a month and pages on its health. The subnet already gave every live pod a unique octet for free.

hints: Hashing 220 names into 1,024 slots collides. What is already unique per live pod?
Something in this cluster already refuses to give two live pods the same value.
Within one /24 subnet, the address allocator already enforces uniqueness.

incidents.title: Ticket server is the signup bottleneck
incidents.brief: Every StreamBox signup asks one MySQL ticket server for the next ID with REPLACE INTO. At 18,000 IDs/s it sits at 94% CPU and signup p95 is 120 ms.
incidents.constraint: IDs may have gaps but must never repeat after a failover.
incidents.question: How do you take the ticket server off the hot path?

users: signup requests 18k/s, 850 failed in the last minute
api: 1 ticket call per signup, no local ID buffer
tix: autoinc lock waits 14 ms avg on a 1-row table

choices.label: Lease blocks of 10,000 IDs per server and hand them out in memory
choices.resultBody: Each API server bumps the counter by 10,000 in one UPDATE and serves IDs locally, so the ticket server sees about 2 writes/s. Cost: a crashed server leaves a gap of unused IDs.

choices.label: Move the counter to Redis INCR with asynchronous replication
choices.resultBody: Redis handles 18,000 INCR/s easily, but a failover promotes a replica a few hundred increments behind, and the next signups receive IDs that already belong to users.

choices.label: Add two read replicas and spread ticket requests across them
choices.resultBody: Every ticket is a write, so only the primary can issue it; the replicas sit idle while the ticket server stays at 94% CPU and signups still wait.

hints: Every signup costs one write on a single row.
Gaps are allowed, so IDs can be reserved ahead.
Reserve many IDs with a single database round trip.

incidents.title: Scraper walked every invoice
incidents.brief: BillFlow invoice links look like /invoice/100234. Over a weekend a scraper incremented the ID and downloaded 2.1M invoices; the IDs also reveal 9,000 new invoices a day to competitors.
incidents.constraint: Internal joins must keep using the BIGINT primary key.
incidents.question: What closes the leak?

choices.label: Check invoice ownership and expose random 128-bit public IDs
choices.resultBody: Ownership checks stop the 2.1M downloads outright, and random public IDs reveal neither order nor volume, while joins keep the internal BIGINT. Cost: one extra indexed lookup per request.

choices.label: Base64-encode the sequential IDs before putting them in links
choices.resultBody: The scraper decodes one link, sees 100234, and resumes incrementing within minutes; the daily invoice count is still readable from the decoded values.

choices.label: Rate-limit invoice pages to 100 requests per minute for each IP
choices.resultBody: Spread across 40,000 addresses the scraper stays under the limit, so the weekend haul barely shrinks, and anyone can still infer volume from two IDs a day apart.

hints: What stops a user from reading someone else's invoice?
Sequential public IDs leak both targets and business volume.
Separate the internal key from what goes in the URL.

incidents.title: Worker-ID leases lapse and ID minting stalls
incidents.brief: RideNow's 3-node etcd leases Snowflake worker IDs from 2-vCPU burstable VMs on gp2 disks. WAL fsync p99 hit 180 ms, heartbeats miss, leases lapse, and ID pods pause minting 14 times an hour.
incidents.constraint: etcd holds only 40 MB of leases, and the lease protocol has never issued a duplicate ID.
incidents.question: What stops the leases from lapsing?

choices.label: Move etcd to larger instances with provisioned-IOPS SSDs

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: The design is sound; the hardware under it was not. Buy the disk before redesigning.

choices.resultTitle: etcd gets the disk it was designed for
choices.resultBody: etcd needs fast, steady fsync on its WAL. On 4-vCPU non-burstable nodes with provisioned-IOPS SSDs, fsync p99 falls to 4 ms, heartbeats land on time and leases stop lapsing. Members were replaced one at a time, so quorum held throughout. Cost: about $350 a month.

choices.label: Raise the worker-ID lease TTL from 10 seconds to 5 minutes
choices.resultBody: The 5-minute TTL rides out most late heartbeats, so minting pauses fall from 14 to 4 an hour. etcd still logs slow-fsync warnings, and the gp2 burst balance is down to 12% and falling.

choices.label: Grow the etcd cluster from 3 to 5 members to share the load
choices.resultBody: Every etcd write must be fsynced by a quorum of 3 out of 5 members, all on the same slow gp2 disks. Nothing is shared out, commit latency rises, and minting pauses climb from 14 to 19 an hour.

hints: The lease logic is correct; look at what etcd needs from its hardware.
Compare the WAL fsync latency with the few milliseconds etcd expects.
Burstable VMs and gp2 volumes both throttle once their credits run out.

variants.constraint: Spend is frozen at $0 until new hardware lands in 3 weeks. Only 220 of 1,024 worker IDs are in use, so a dead pod's ID can sit leased for minutes.

long-ttl.resultTitle: Five-minute leases outlast every fsync stall
long-ttl.resultBody: Renewing every 10 seconds, a 5-minute lease survives 30 missed heartbeats, so 180 ms fsync spikes no longer lapse it. Pauses drop to under 1 an hour for $0; a crashed pod's ID stays reserved 5 minutes, harmless with 800 spare.

upsize.resultBody: Provisioned-IOPS instances would fix fsync, but they add $350 a month during a $0 freeze, and the hardware arriving in 3 weeks replaces them anyway. While the request waits, leases keep lapsing 14 times an hour.

hints: The disk stays slow for 3 weeks. What decides how long a hiccup can last before a lease is lost?
A lease only lapses when renewals fail for its whole lifetime.
With 800 spare worker IDs, holding a dead pod's ID longer costs almost nothing.

incidents.title: Order pages open the wrong order
incidents.brief: Snowflake order IDs are live. Web and Android parse JSON numbers as doubles, exact only to 2^53, so order IDs arrive rounded to a multiple of 256. 70% of order-page loads now 404.
incidents.constraint: The web app ships daily and Android can force an update; the order key stays a 64-bit BIGINT.
incidents.question: What gets every client the exact order ID?

choices.label: Add an id_str string field and switch clients to it
choices.resultBody: JSON strings are never rounded, so the web app and the forced Android update read id_str and every order page resolves; old clients keep the numeric id until they update. Cost: each ID is sent twice, about 20 bytes.

choices.label: Shift the Snowflake epoch so new IDs stay below 2^53
choices.resultBody: Fitting under 2^53 leaves 31 bits of milliseconds beside the 22 worker and sequence bits, about 24 days before the timestamp wraps and IDs repeat. The orders already minted still 404.

choices.label: Parse responses with a BigInt-aware JSON library on web
choices.resultBody: The web app now reads exact IDs, but Android's JSON parser still turns them into doubles, so about 40% of order-page loads keep returning 404 or someone else's order.

hints: What is the largest integer a double holds exactly?
The server sends the right number; the client's parser changes it.
Text survives any JSON parser untouched.

incidents.title: Welcome emails skip 4% of signups
incidents.brief: With leased ID blocks live, the welcome-email job polls WHERE id > last_seen. Server C hands out 40,xxx while server B still hands out 30,xxx, so B's signups are skipped: 4% never verify.
incidents.constraint: The ticket server stays off the hot path and blocks stay at 10,000 IDs.
incidents.question: How should the job find users it hasn't emailed yet?

choices.label: Poll a partial index of users where welcomed is false
choices.resultBody: The job now asks for rows still marked welcomed=false through a small partial index and flips the flag after sending, so ID order no longer matters. Cost: one extra UPDATE per signup.

choices.label: Shrink ID blocks from 10,000 to 100 so servers stay close
choices.resultBody: Servers now drift only a few hundred IDs apart, but the cursor still overtakes the slowest block, skips fall only to about 1%, and the ticket server climbs to 180 writes/s.

choices.label: Rescan the whole users table nightly for missed signups
choices.resultBody: Skipped users do get an email, but up to 24 hours late, after most have given up, and the 90M-row scan pins the Users DB at 85% CPU for an hour every night.

hints: With leased blocks, is ID order still signup order?
A cursor on id assumes every new row gets a bigger id.
Track which rows still need work, not how far you got.

incidents.title: etcd leader flaps and new pods get no worker ID
incidents.brief: The 5-minute lease TTL bought 50 minutes. Then etcd's gp2 burst credits ran out: WAL fsync p99 is 900 ms, the leader changed 6 times, and 40 new ID pods can't get a lease.
incidents.constraint: Pods may never mint without a lease; a duplicate trip ID is worse than a stall.
incidents.question: What gets etcd committing on time again?

choices.label: Swap each etcd member onto a provisioned-IOPS SSD in turn
choices.resultBody: Replacing one member at a time keeps quorum while each moves to a volume with guaranteed IOPS; fsync p99 falls to 5 ms, the leader settles and the 40 waiting pods get leases. Cost: about $300 a month.

choices.label: Raise etcd heartbeat and election timeouts tenfold to stop flaps
choices.resultBody: The leader stops flapping, but every lease grant still waits on a 900 ms fsync, and a real leader crash now takes 10 s to detect; the new pods keep queueing for IDs.

choices.label: Let pods mint with random worker IDs until etcd recovers
choices.resultBody: A random worker ID can land on any of the 220 IDs already leased to live pods, so within minutes duplicate trip IDs reach the trips DB and the lease system's one guarantee is gone.

hints: The longer TTL hid the symptom; the disk never changed.
gp2 volumes drop to baseline IOPS once burst credits run out.
etcd's commit speed is bounded by its disk's fsync latency.

incidents.title: NTP clock step backwards halts Snowflake ID generation
incidents.brief: An unscheduled NTP time synchronization steps system clocks backwards by 80ms, causing Snowflake workers to reject ID generation to avoid duplicate keys.
incidents.constraint: Preserve unique 64-bit integer IDs without failing client requests during clock adjustments.
incidents.question: How should Snowflake generators handle backwards clock drift safely?

choices.label: Pause thread execution until clock catches up or switch NTP to slew mode
choices.resultTitle: NTP slewing and spin-pause prevented ID collision
choices.resultBody: Slewing adjusts time gradually without backward steps; brief spin-pausing handles millisecond jitter without failing requests.

choices.label: Ignore the backward clock step and continue generating duplicate timestamps
choices.resultTitle: Reused timestamps caused duplicate primary key violations
choices.resultBody: Generating IDs with backwards timestamps caused sequence collisions with previously issued keys, corrupting orders.

choices.label: Fallback to generating pseudo-random 32-bit integers during clock drift
choices.resultTitle: 32-bit random integers produced massive birthday paradox collisions
choices.resultBody: Random 32-bit integers suffer birthday attacks at just tens of thousands of requests, colliding on database insert.

hints: Snowflake relies on monotonically advancing timestamps to prevent ID reuse.
NTP step adjustments jump time backwards, whereas NTP slewing gradually speeds or slows tick rates.
Short backwards drift can be absorbed by brief busy-wait spinning until time passes the last recorded millisecond.

incidents.title: Random UUIDv4 primary keys cause database page fragmentation
incidents.brief: An e-commerce order table with 100M rows indexed by random UUIDv4 suffers extreme B-Tree leaf page splits, quadrupling storage size and slowing inserts.
incidents.constraint: Maintain globally unique IDs generated without coordination, but preserve sequential insert locality.
incidents.question: Which ID format provides decentralized generation while maintaining time-ordered locality?

choices.label: Migrate primary keys to UUIDv7 with millisecond timestamp prefixes
choices.resultTitle: UUIDv7 restored sequential B-Tree append locality
choices.resultBody: UUIDv7 embeds Unix timestamps in the most significant bits, turning random inserts into sequential appends on B-Tree leaf pages.

choices.label: Double database server RAM so the entire fragmented index fits in cache
choices.resultTitle: Adding RAM delayed but did not fix ongoing page split bloat
choices.resultBody: The index continued to fragment as table size expanded, quickly outpacing the new memory capacity and inflating monthly bills.

choices.label: Hash UUIDv4 keys with SHA-256 before inserting into the primary table
choices.resultTitle: Hashing keys increased CPU load without fixing randomness
choices.resultBody: Cryptographic hashing produces uniformly distributed output, maintaining the exact same random insertion pattern.

hints: UUIDv4 is 122 bits of pure randomness, scattering inserts across the entire B-Tree.
UUIDv7 and ULID combine a 48-bit timestamp prefix with random entropy bits.
Time-prefixed IDs write sequentially to the rightmost leaf page, eliminating 95% of splits.

incidents.title: Sequence bit exhaustion during sub-millisecond flash sale burst
incidents.brief: A single Snowflake worker instance receives 6,000 requests in 0.8ms during a flash sale, exhausting its 12-bit sequence counter (4,096 max IDs/ms).
incidents.constraint: Handle traffic spikes exceeding 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node without ID collision.
incidents.question: How should Snowflake generators handle sequence overflow within a single millisecond?

choices.label: Block and spin-wait until the next millisecond tick or distribute worker IDs
choices.resultTitle: Spin-waiting to next millisecond prevented sequence wrap
choices.resultBody: When the 12-bit sequence counter fills, spinning until the clock advances by 1ms safely resets the sequence counter without collisions.

choices.label: Wrap sequence counter back to zero immediately within the same millisecond
choices.resultTitle: Sequence wrap caused catastrophic duplicate IDs
choices.resultBody: Wrapping the sequence counter within the same millisecond produced duplicate IDs, violating database primary key constraints.

choices.label: Reject excess requests with HTTP 429 and instruct clients to back off
choices.resultTitle: Excessive client rejections caused high checkout abandonment
choices.resultBody: Failing user orders when a 1ms spin-wait would have succeeded caused massive revenue loss during the flash sale.

hints: A 12-bit sequence allows 4,096 IDs per millisecond per generator node.
If 4,096 IDs are exhausted in under 1ms, the generator must pause until the clock ticks to the next millisecond.
Scaling horizontally with distinct worker IDs spreads throughput across nodes.

incidents.title: Centralized ticket server database crash halts order processing
incidents.brief: A centralized MySQL Ticket Server using REPLACE INTO to issue sequential auto-increment IDs crashes under high lock contention, freezing checkout.
incidents.constraint: Remove single point of failure in ID allocation while preserving monotonic ordering.
incidents.question: How should centralized ticket servers be replaced for high availability?

choices.label: Allocate chunked ID ranges in memory (e.g. 5,000 IDs per worker lease)
choices.resultTitle: Chunked range allocations eliminated database contention
choices.resultBody: Workers fetch blocks of IDs in a single atomic transaction and serve them locally from RAM, reducing database calls by 99.9%.

choices.label: Deploy read replicas to serve REPLACE INTO tickets concurrently
choices.resultTitle: Replicas cannot handle write ticket auto-increments
choices.resultBody: Read replicas cannot execute auto-increment ticket writes without causing massive duplicate IDs and replication divergence.

choices.label: Configure clients to retry ticket server queries with infinite loops
choices.resultTitle: Infinite retries completed a full thundering herd outage
choices.resultBody: Client connection pools filled up and crashed all application tiers trying to talk to the dead ticket database.

hints: Flickr ticket servers used auto-increment with step offsets, but centralized databases remain bottlenecks.
Chunking or leasing ID ranges (e.g. Hi/Lo algorithm) serves IDs from memory.
A single round trip to the database can provision 10,000 IDs for an application pod.

incidents.title: Worker ID collision after autoscaling Kubernetes pod restart
incidents.brief: During a horizontal scale-out event, two new worker pods read the same static worker_id configuration, producing conflicting IDs in production.
incidents.constraint: Ensure dynamic, conflict-free worker ID assignment without static pod configuration.
incidents.question: How should worker node IDs be coordinated dynamically in autoscaling clusters?

choices.label: Acquire ephemeral worker ID leases from etcd or Consul on pod startup
choices.resultTitle: Dynamic coordinator lease prevented worker ID overlap
choices.resultBody: Dynamic coordination through etcd/Consul guarantees each pod registers a strictly unique worker ID that expires if the pod dies.

choices.label: Assign random worker IDs between 1 and 1024 without any coordination
choices.resultTitle: Random worker IDs frequently collided due to birthday paradox
choices.resultBody: With only 1024 worker slots, running dozens of pods created an unacceptable 50%+ probability of identical worker IDs.

choices.label: Truncate pod IP addresses and use low-order bytes as worker IDs
choices.resultTitle: Truncated IP octets collided across different subnet blocks
choices.resultBody: Pods on different CIDR subnets shared identical low-order bytes (e.g. 10.0.1.15 and 10.0.2.15), leading to ID duplication.

hints: Snowflake allocates 10 bits for worker/datacenter IDs (up to 1,024 nodes).
Hardcoding worker IDs in config maps or environment variables fails during auto-scaling.
Coordination services provide atomic, ephemeral sequential leases for pod registration.

incidents.title: Orders fail with duplicate primary keys since the 14:10 deploy
incidents.brief: INSERT on orders.id violates the unique constraint 340 times a minute. IDs are 64-bit Snowflake values. Clock offset is 3 ms, and the order service went from 24 to 64 pods in the same window.
incidents.constraint: Only one revert can ship before the evening peak.
incidents.question: Which PR do you revert to stop the duplicate IDs?

choices.label: Revert PR #5810: chrony poll interval from 16 s to 64 s
choices.diff:
ops/chrony.conf
-server ntp.internal poll 4
+server ntp.internal poll 6
 # 2^4 = 16 s, 2^6 = 64 s
choices.resultBody: Polling NTP less often could add a few ms of drift, but offset is 3 ms and the library refuses to move backwards. Duplicates continue at 335 a minute because pods still share worker IDs.

choices.label: Revert PR #5822: fetch 100 IDs per SDK call instead of 1
choices.diff:
sdk/ids.go
-const idBlockSize = 1
+const idBlockSize = 100
 // one call reserves a block of sequence numbers
choices.resultBody: Allocating 100 IDs at a time changes call count, not uniqueness: each block is still stamped with its pod's worker ID. Reverting it leaves 340 duplicates a minute and adds 5,900 extra calls a second.

choices.label: Revert PR #5834: worker_id from hostname hash, not a lease
choices.diff:
idgen/config.go
 # PR #5834: drop the lease service call at boot
-workerID = registry.Lease(podName)
+workerID = hash(hostname) % 1024
 bits: 41 time | 10 worker | 12 seq
choices.resultTitle: Each pod holds its own worker ID again
choices.resultBody: Hashing hostnames into 1,024 slots collides once 64 pods are running: the birthday odds of a shared slot are about 87%. Two pods with one worker ID and the same millisecond emit the same ID. The lease hands out unique IDs, so duplicates drop to 0. Cost: a lease call at pod start-up.

hints: Clock offset is fine, so look at what makes two IDs the same.
Snowflake IDs collide only when time, worker and sequence all match.
Which diff lets two pods end up with the same worker bits?

incidents.title: ID service costs $7,200 a month to hand out 9k IDs a second
incidents.brief: Nine ID pods across three zones each run 4% CPU at 1k IDs/s of a 40k/s capacity. The lease registry uses 6%. Finance asks for a cut; the service has never emitted a duplicate.
incidents.constraint: IDs must stay unique and generation must survive the loss of one zone.
incidents.question: Which cut saves money without breaking the SLO?

choices.label: Delete the lease registry and hardcode worker IDs in config
choices.resultBody: The registry is at 6% CPU, but it is what stops two pods sharing a worker ID. With static config a scale-out clones an ID, and the first shared millisecond emits duplicate keys: 90 collisions a minute in the first hour.

choices.label: Cut ID pods from 9 to 4 and keep them spread over 3 zones
choices.resultBody: Load is 9k IDs/s against 40k per pod. Four pods share 2.25k IDs/s each, about 6% of capacity, and losing one zone leaves at least 2 pods handling 4.5k IDs/s each, still 11% CPU. The bill falls by roughly $2,100. Cost: less headroom for a 10x launch spike.

choices.label: Consolidate all ID pods into one zone to drop cross-zone traffic
choices.resultTitle: One zone outage stops every order
choices.resultBody: Cross-zone traffic is small at 9k IDs/s, but the zone loss is not: with all pods in one zone an outage means no IDs issued, so checkout fails until pods restart elsewhere, about 6 minutes against a 99.95% budget of 22 minutes a month.

hints: Everything is green, so ask what each part protects and what it costs to lose it.
Utilisation says how much you can remove; the failure it prevents says what you cannot.
Which part is mostly idle but not the one that keeps IDs unique or zone-proof?

incidents.title: Order IDs open the wrong order in the browser
incidents.brief: AdminWeb reads order IDs as JavaScript numbers, so 63-bit Snowflake IDs lose their low bits and 1 in 1,800 orders opens the wrong record. A 53-bit layout leaves 12 bits after the 41-bit timestamp.
incidents.constraint: Partners parse IDs as JSON numbers, so string IDs are out; all 20 pods may burst to 40 IDs per millisecond.
incidents.question: How many of the 12 spare bits go to the per-millisecond sequence?

choices.label: Fit IDs in 53 bits: 41 timestamp, 6 worker, 6 sequence
choices.resultBody: Six worker bits allow 64 pods and six sequence bits give each pod 64 IDs per ms, so 20 pods and 40-ID bursts fit and every ID parses exactly. Cost: a pod tops out at 64k IDs/s, and 41 timestamp bits last about 70 years from a custom epoch.

choices.label: Serialize IDs as strings in the admin API response only
choices.resultBody: The admin UI is fixed, but partner CSV exports and webhooks still carry 63-bit numbers that their tools parse as doubles, so about 1 in 1,800 partner lookups keeps hitting the wrong order.

choices.label: Use one Redis INCR counter as the whole 53-bit ID
choices.resultBody: IDs stay numeric and small, but with asynchronous replication a failover can rewind the counter 1-2 seconds and re-issue about 40,000 IDs, and every create now pays a 0.5 ms Redis round trip.

addNodes.label: Redis INCR
addNodes.sub: async replica, ID rewind on failover

hints: A browser number is a 64-bit float: only 53 bits are exact.
The timestamp keeps 41 bits; worker ID and sequence share what is left.
Count pods needing worker IDs, then count IDs one pod mints in a millisecond; both must fit.

knob.label: Sequence bits
knob.question: Set how many of the 12 spare bits go to the sequence; the rest identify the worker.

low.title: Bursts wait for the next millisecond
low.body: At 5 sequence bits or fewer a pod mints at most 32 IDs per ms, so a 40-ID burst stalls, and at 0 bits the last ID waits 39 ms for the clock to tick.

high.title: Pods cannot get a worker ID
high.body: At 8 sequence bits or more only 16 or fewer worker IDs exist, so at least 4 of the 20 pods are refused at startup and, at 12 bits, 19 of them cannot start.

good.title: Both limits fit in 12 bits
good.body: At 6 or 7 sequence bits there are 32 to 64 worker IDs for 20 pods and 64 to 128 IDs per ms per pod, so bursts of 40 never wait and no pod is refused.
